newsitem.title: BELGIUM: European Commission welcomes Cuba law suspension.
newsitem.headline: European Commission welcomes Cuba law suspension.

text.p: The European Commission on Friday welcomed news that the United States will further suspend the introduction of a law allowing Americans to sue foreigners with certain investments in Cuba.
But European Commission President Jacques Santer said the EU would only be entirely satisfied when Washington completely scrapped the so-called Helms-Burton Act.
"I welcome this initiative as a constructive move ... a step in the right direction," said Santer in a statement.

"I should point out, however, that today's announcement does not change the European Union's position of principle ... that we remain firmly opposed to all extraterritorial legislation, whatever its source, and will continue to defend our interests."

The Helms-Burton act, an amalgamation of decades of U.S. anti-Cuba legislation, was passed in early 1996 to a chorus of indignation from EU members and other nations opposed to what they termed its extra-territorial nature.

Among other things, the act allows naturalised Americans to sue in U.S. courts foreign individuals or companies deemed to have profited from investing in property confiscated by the Cuban government since the communist revolution of 1959.
In July, U.S. President Bill Clinton said he would suspend this part of the act for six months to give a special envoy time to win support for Washington's anti-Cuba policy.
On Friday, Clinton said he would suspend it for a further six months after receiving assurances from the EU and other American allies that they were working to help bring democracy to Cuba.

The EU has argued in the past that it is already engaged in constructive efforts to bring about change in Cuba and passed a law in October making it illegal for European companies or individuals to comply with the U.S. act.
The EU also formally raised the matter at the World Trade Organisation (WTO) and a disputes settlement panel was formed in December to look into the case.
Other parts of the Helms-Burton Act prohibit individuals with links to companies deemed to have invested in propertry confiscated from American citizens from travelling to the U.S.

This has already barred European executives from Canadian mining conglomerate Sheritt International and Spanish hotels and tourism chain Sol Melia from visiting the U.S. since June. Officials from Mexico's Grupo Domos have also been barred.
